subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: copying and pasting code without understanding [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Afreen, and I share the lab computer with Faisal. His Python homework was a program to average marks, and it ran perfectly. He had pasted it from a forum. Then the teacher said, “Add a line to ignore any zero mark.” Faisal stared at the screen for a long time. He tried another forum snippet; the program crashed. He scrolled up and down and muttered, “I don't know what line six does.” I can't be sure how he felt, but his ears went red. He stayed after school to redo it and missed his bus. I noticed that the code had looked so clever at first, and fell apart the moment anyone touched it.

qa.q: What was Faisal's homework program supposed to do?
How did Faisal probably feel when the teacher asked for a small change?
qa.a: Embarrassed and stuck: he stared at the screen and his ears went red, though Afreen cannot be certain of his feelings.

qa.q: What could Faisal do instead of pasting, and why?
qa.a: Read each pasted line, write what it does in his own words and change one thing at a time, since knowing why a line is there lets him modify it.

qa.q: How does the pasted program look to Afreen?
qa.a: Afreen sees it work at first and then fail at the smallest change, so it seems clever but hollow.

grounding: A student pastes forum answers until the program runs, then cannot modify it because he never understood the lines.

subtype: Approach: copying and pasting code without understanding [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday: Pranav's computer project, a program that splits the class into teams at random, keeps crashing. He copies a block from a forum answer. New error. He pastes a second answer over part of the first. Near midnight it finally runs, and he texts Kunal, “Done!! 😅”
Thursday: Ma'am asks for one change: teams of five instead of four. Pranav opens the file. Twenty-six lines, and he can't say what half of them do. He changes a 4 to a 5. Now the program leaves three students out entirely. He tries another forum answer; it breaks something else.
The following Monday: The project goes in late, with marks cut. Kunal, who wrote his own shorter version, sits with Pranav after school, and they go through the code one line at a time, asking, “Why is this here?”

qa.q: What change did Ma'am ask for on Thursday?
qa.a: Teams of five instead of four.

qa.q: What was Pranav probably feeling on Thursday when he couldn't explain half the lines?
qa.a: He was likely panicky and ashamed, because the program he thought was finished had become something he could not control 😰

qa.q: What else could Pranav have done on Monday night instead of stacking forum answers?
qa.a: Paste one answer, then change a small part of it and see what happens, so each line is understood before the next is added.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Pranav's situation by the following Monday?
qa.a: Kunal might see that the slower, shorter version written by hand was the stronger one, and wants Pranav to understand the code rather than just patch it.

grounding: Shows a student pasting forum code until it runs, then failing to make a small change because he never understood why the lines were there.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: copying and pasting code without understanding [Pitfall]
passage:
Tejas, you asked why I make you explain every line. Sit, I'll tell you.
When I was in Class Eleven, our school had one computer lab, and there was an internet café down the road. I had to build a small library record program. I found forum posts, pasted them together, and after three evenings it ran. Our teacher, Fernandes Sir, looked at it and said, “Chaitanya, good. Now make it show only the books that are overdue.”
One small change. I sat there till the lab closed. I didn't know which line did what, because I had never once asked why any of them was there.
Fernandes Sir didn't scold. He made me rebuild it slowly, one piece at a time, explaining each piece to him before writing the next. It took two weeks.
So that is why your uncle asks “why” so much.

qa.q: What small change did Fernandes Sir ask for?
qa.a: To make the program show only the books that are overdue.

qa.q: What was young Chaitanya feeling while sitting in the lab until it closed?
qa.a: He was likely stuck and embarrassed, because a program that seemed finished could not be changed at all.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned things around for Chaitanya?
qa.a: Rebuilding the program slowly, one piece at a time, and explaining each piece to Fernandes Sir; understanding replaced pasting.

qa.q: How might Fernandes Sir have seen the pasted program?
qa.a: The teacher probably suspected it was not really understood and used one small change to reveal that, without scolding.

grounding: An uncle recalls pasting forum answers into a school program that ran but could not be changed, since no line had been understood.
